title: Effects of post-planting management practices on early Acacia mearnsii stand development and biomass carbon stock in drylands
content:
by Abrha Brhan Gebre, Emiru Birhane, Niguse Hagazi, Mulat Kebede, Amos Enock Majule, Edmond Alavaisha

Land degradation severely depletes dryland biomass carbon, yet the capacity and effectiveness of post-planting interventions involving nitrogen-fixing species for climate mitigation remain poorly quantified. This study evaluated the individual and interactive effects of management practices and planting pit sizes on early-stand biomass carbon allocation and predicted soil variables associated with biomass carbon over a two‑year timeline. Acacia mearnsii plantations were monitored under a factorial combination of two pit sizes (30 and 50 cm) and four management regimes: an unmanaged control; watering alone (W); watering with mulching (WM); and integrated watering, mulching, and compost (WMC). Biomass carbon was quantified using destructive sampling and analyzed using generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). Comprehensive multivariate soil property matrices were simultaneously analyzed across management interventions using R software. Management significantly increased biomass carbon (χ2 = 42.62, p < 0.001), whereas planting pit size had no significant independent effect. The unmanaged control averaged the lowest total biomass at 47 t CO2e ha-1, whereas WMC achieved a maximum mean of 140 t CO2e ha-1, followed by 116 and 88.4 t CO2e ha-1 for WM and W, respectively, in two years. Predictive models demonstrated that Na+, total nitrogen and Available phosphorus explained variance in carbon allocation. Adding WMC reduces soil bulk density and enhances biomass carbon, implying carbon sequestration potential. Root carbon linked with sodium concentration suggests soil chemistry plays a role in carbon allocation and stress buffering. The integrated management (WMC) regime combined with a 50 cm pit size is recommended as the most effective restoration practice in tropical drylands, as this treatment produced the highest aboveground and total biomass carbon stock gains.
